entries.meaning: A clipped spoken form of alright, strongly associated with African American English and with casual urban speech generally. It works as agreement, as an acknowledgment, and as a check-in question (You aight?), and it sounds badly out of place in any professional setting.
examples: "You want me to grab you a plate?" "Aight, thanks."
Aight, I'm heading out — text me when you land.
"We're meeting at seven instead of six." "Aight, cool."
"Aight, aight, I hear you. I'll stop bringing it up."
He just nodded and said "a'ight" and went back to his game.

variants: all right (the traditional two-word spelling, still preferred in edited prose)
entries.meaning: A general-purpose yes that also works as a transition. As agreement it is warmer than fine and less committed than absolutely; at the front of a turn it often just means "I'm moving us along now."
examples: "Can you be there by nine?" "Alright, nine works."
Alright, everybody, let's get started.
"I'll pay you back Friday." "All right, but don't forget again."
Alright, fair point — I hadn't thought about the shipping cost.
"Alright!" he said, clapping his hands. "Who's driving?"

entries.meaning: The most widely usable agreement token in American English: it fits a boardroom, a text message, and a hospital form. It accepts, it acknowledges, and — with falling intonation and a pause — it signals a shift to the next thing. In texting, a bare k often reads as cold or annoyed, so people write ok or kk instead.
examples: "Meeting's been pushed to Thursday." "Okay, I'll update the calendar."
Okay, so where were we?
"Don't touch anything until I get back." "Okay, okay."
She texted back a single "ok" and I spent an hour wondering what I'd done.
"Okey-dokey," my grandfather said, "let's see what's under the hood."

entries.meaning: An easy, low-effort yes, most natural as an answer to a request or an offer. Tone does all the work: a bright sure is genuinely willing, a flat one is grudging, and a drawn-out suuure means the speaker does not believe a word of it.
examples: "Could you cover my shift Saturday?" "Sure, no problem."
"Want some coffee?" "Sure, thanks."
"Is it okay if I bring my roommate?" "Sure, the more the merrier."
"I was going to call you." "Suuure you were."
"Sure, sure, whatever you say," he muttered, clearly done arguing.

entries.meaning: A friendly, upbeat yes to a request, and the standard cheerful American answer to thank you. It is the sort of thing waiters, coworkers, and neighbors say; it would be too breezy in a formal reply to a client.
examples: "Can you send me that file when you get a chance?" "Sure thing."
"Thanks for holding the elevator." "Sure thing."
"Mind if I borrow your charger?" "Sure thing, it's in my bag."
"Sure thing, boss — I'll have it on your desk by noon."
"Sure thing," the guy behind the counter said, and had it boxed up before I finished the sentence.

entries.meaning: The default spoken yes in American English — so ordinary that a full yes in casual talk can sound stiff or pointed. 1. Plain agreement or affirmation. 2. Doubled or tripled (yeah, yeah, yeah), it turns impatient: "I've heard this already, move on."
examples: "Are you coming to the thing tonight?" "Yeah, I'll be there around eight."
Yeah, that's exactly what I was thinking.
"You've seen this movie, right?" "Yeah, like four times."
"Yeah, yeah, yeah — I know, I should have checked the oil."
"Did it hurt?" "Yeah, more than I expected, honestly."

entries.meaning: A crisp, closed-off yes, ending in a popped p. It confirms efficiently and often signals that the speaker considers the matter settled — which can read as brisk or slightly cold if the other person wanted more.
examples: "Is this the line for tickets?" "Yep."
"So you already sent it?" "Yup, this morning."
"Yep, that's the one," she said, pointing at the blue folder.
"You're sure you locked the door?" "Yep. Checked twice."
"Sounds like a long drive." "Yep. Nine hours, no stops."

entries.meaning: The full, unreduced affirmative. In American speech it carries weight: people use it for formal answers, for emphasis, and when a casual yeah would sound too loose — under oath, in an interview, when correcting a misunderstanding, or when they really mean it.
examples: "Do you swear to tell the truth?" "Yes, I do."
"Yes, I'm absolutely certain. I saw the email myself."
"Would you like the receipt?" "Yes, please."
"Are you saying we're over budget?" "Yes. By about nine thousand."
"Yes sir, I'll take care of it first thing."

entries.meaning: A hearty American yes with a Midwestern and Western flavor. It answers a question with enthusiasm and, like sure thing, doubles as a warm reply to thank you. You betcha is folksier still and can sound like a deliberate impression of the Upper Midwest.
examples: "Will you be at the game Sunday?" "You bet."
"Thanks for all your help today." "You bet, anytime."
"Is the fishing any good up there?" "You betcha. Best walleye in the state."
"Can you have it done by Friday?" "You bet — Thursday, even."
"You think she'll win?" "You bet she will."

entries.meaning: Total, unqualified agreement — the modern replacement for absolutely among younger speakers. It says not just "yes" but "I have no reservations whatsoever."
examples: "We should just cancel and reschedule." "One hundred percent."
A hundred percent — that place has gone downhill since they changed owners.
"Do you think I should take the job?" "A hundred percent. Don't overthink it."
"It's not really about the money, is it?" "One hundred percent not."
"A hundred percent agree with everything you just said."

entries.meaning: Emphatic yes with no hedging. It works at every level of formality, which makes it one of the most useful upgrades from a plain yes — warm in conversation, professional in an email, forceful in a meeting.
examples: "Is that number final?" "Absolutely. We double-checked it."
"Would you recommend her?" "Absolutely — she's the best hire we made last year."
"Can I quote you on that?" "Absolutely, go ahead."
"Absolutely," the doctor said. "That's a completely normal reaction to the medication."
"You'd do it again?" "Absolutely. In a heartbeat."

entries.meaning: Warm, folksy agreement with a weary or hard-won observation. The nonstandard ain't is doing deliberate work here: Americans who never otherwise say ain't say this, because the whole point is to sound plainspoken. It answers complaints and rueful truths, never questions.
examples: "Everything costs twice what it did five years ago." "Ain't that the truth."
"Ain't that the truth," my aunt said, and went back to her crossword.
"Nobody's job is safe anymore." "Ain't that the truth. Ask me how I know."
"You can't fix a bad manager with a better spreadsheet." "Ain't it the truth."
"Kids grow up while you're busy looking at your phone." "Ain't that the truth, unfortunately."

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hebrew by way of church liturgy, where it closes a prayer with "so be it." Outside of worship it is fervent agreement with something someone just said, usually a complaint or a hard truth, and it carries a faint pulpit echo that speakers use half-jokingly.
examples: "Whoever designed this parking lot should be ashamed." "Amen."
"Amen to that," she said, raising her glass.
"All I want is one weekend with nothing on the calendar." "Amen, brother."
The congregation answered amen and the organ started up.
"Kids should be outside, not on screens all day." "Amen. Can I get an amen?"

entries.meaning: Current American youth slang, from African American English, meaning "agreed," "understood," or "it's a deal." It answers a plan with confirmation and is common in texts among people under about thirty-five; from a manager to a client it would land as strange.
examples: "Meet me at the courts at six." "Bet."
"I'll Venmo you tonight." "Bet, thanks."
"You're not gonna finish that whole thing." "Bet." (here: a challenge — "watch me")
"Party's moved to Danny's place." "Bet, see you there."
"Bet," he texted back, and that was the whole conversation.

entries.meaning: From the game, where it announces a winning card. As agreement it means "you have hit the exact answer," and it is usually said when the other person names the very thing the speaker was fishing for. It is upbeat and a little theatrical — right for a whiteboard, wrong for a condolence call.
examples: "So the charge only shows up after the free trial ends?" "Bingo."
"Bingo — that's the file I've been hunting for all morning."
"Wait. Is it because both accounts use the same email?" "Bingo."
"Bingo!" the teacher said. "That's exactly the word I was after."
"You think he's stalling because he never ordered the parts?" "Bingo. Give the man a prize."

entries.meaning: A polished, slightly formal yes. It is the standard register of hotel desks, customer service, and professional correspondence; between friends it can sound stilted or faintly sarcastic.
examples: "Could you send someone up with extra towels?" "Certainly, ma'am."
"Certainly. I'll have the revised contract to you this afternoon."
"May I ask a follow-up question?" "Certainly."
"Would that be a problem for your team?" "Certainly not."
"So you're the expert on all this now?" "Certainly," he said, in a voice that meant the opposite.

variants: darn right / dang right (the clean substitutes)
entries.meaning: Forceful agreement with a note of defiance in it — not merely "yes" but "yes, and I dare you to argue." Damn sits at the mild end of American profanity, but it is profanity: unremarkable among friends or in a bar, and conspicuous in a meeting, a classroom, or anywhere somebody's kids are listening. Darn right and dang right carry the same punch at no risk.
examples: "You're going to ask for the raise, aren't you?" "Damn right I am."
"Damn straight. I'm not paying forty dollars to park."
"That was a foul." "Damn right it was."
"You'd have done the same for me." "Darn right I would."
"So you told him no?" "Damn right I did, and I'd tell him again tomorrow."

variants: defo (rare in the U.S., mostly British)
definately (a very common misspelling — avoid it)
entries.meaning: Confident agreement, with a shade more "I'm sure about this" than "I'm enthusiastic about this." It is the everyday middle ground between a plain yes and a booming absolutely.
examples: "Should we book ahead?" "Definitely. It fills up on weekends."
"Definitely the best burger in town."
"Are you in for Saturday?" "Definitely, put me down for two."
"You think that's a typo?" "Definitely. That can't be the real price."
"Am I making that up, or was he there too?" "Definitely there. He drove."

entries.meaning: The standard way to endorse someone else's point rather than answer their question. It means "you have put your finger on it," and it is the single most useful agreement token in a discussion or an argument where you want to align yourself with the last speaker. It is also an ordinary adverb, so watch the boundary: Exactly how much are we talking about? is a real question, while a standalone Exactly. is agreement.
examples: "So the problem isn't the code, it's the data." "Exactly."
"Exactly — that's the part nobody wants to talk about."
"You're saying we'd have to redo the whole thing?" "Exactly right."
"She wasn't angry, she was embarrassed." "Exactly. That's what I've been trying to say."
"Exactly!" three people said at once, and the meeting finally moved on.

entries.meaning: Internet-era and African American English agreement meaning "what you just said is simply true." It is a full turn on its own and is extremely common in comments, group chats, and casual speech among younger Americans.
examples: "Nobody's checking email at eleven at night." "Facts."
"Facts — that album has not aged well."
"Rent in this city is completely out of control." "Facts."
She replied to his post with one word: "facts."
"You can't out-train a bad diet." "Facts. Learned that the hard way."

entries.meaning: 1. As a reply it endorses what was just said as the honest truth, close to facts. 2. With rising intonation, for real? is genuine surprise — the casual cousin of really?. The doubled for real for real, written frfr in texts, insists that the speaker is not exaggerating at all.
examples: "Nobody in this office knows how the printer works." "For real."
"He drove eleven hours straight without stopping." "For real?"
"For real, that is the last time I let him plan a trip."
"I'm putting in my notice at the end of the month." "For real? Since when?"
"Frfr," she texted, "I have not slept in two days."

variants: fo sho (very informal, African American English)
entries.meaning: Relaxed, confident agreement — a little more emphatic than sure and a little more casual than definitely. It also tags onto the end of a statement to underline it (It's cold out, for sure).
examples: "Are you going to the reunion?" "For sure. Wouldn't miss it."
"It's cheaper to fly out of the other airport, for sure."
"You'll let me know either way?" "For sure."
"Fo sho," he laughed. "I'll be there at eight."
"That was the loudest concert I've ever been to." "For sure. My ears are still ringing."

variants: here here (a common misspelling — the word is hear)
entries.meaning: A shout of public agreement inherited from British parliamentary practice, short for "hear him, hear him." Americans use it at toasts, at meetings, and in comment threads, often with a knowing formality; said in a small private conversation it sounds like a joke.
examples: "To another twenty-five years of marriage." "Hear, hear!"
"Hear, hear," someone called from the back of the room.
The board members murmured hear, hear as she finished her statement.
"Anyone who fixes this parking situation gets my vote." "Hear, hear."
Half the replies under the article were some version of "hear, hear."

entries.meaning: Loud, delighted agreement. It expresses excitement as much as assent. Hell is at the mild end of American profanity, but it is still profanity: harmless among friends, noticeable in a classroom, a client meeting, or a room with somebody's grandmother in it. Heck yeah carries the same energy with none of the risk.
examples: "Want to go see them play Friday?" "Hell yeah I do."
"Hell yeah!" the whole bar yelled when the shot went in.
"Free food in the break room." "Heck yeah."
"Are you proud of her?" "Hell yes. She worked two years for this."
"They finally fixed the elevator." "Heck yeah they did. Only took eight months."

entries.meaning: Emphatic agreement with an understatement: "you're right, and if anything you're putting it mildly." It has a mid-century flavor and comes more readily from older Americans, but it has never gone away, and it is nearly always said with a short laugh.
examples: "That was a long meeting." "I'll say. Two and a half hours."
"Looks like it rained a little." "I'll say! There's an inch of water in the basement."
"She seems pretty happy about the news." "I'll say she is."
"I'll say," my father muttered. "Cheapest car he ever bought and the best one."
"The hill's a little steep at the end." "I'll say. I had to walk the bike up."

entries.meaning: A dignified yes that confirms and slightly elevates. In American English it is noticeably bookish; used in ordinary chat it reads as either erudite or deliberately arch, which is exactly why people use it for comic effect.
examples: "This is the original 1912 edition?" "Indeed it is."
"Indeed," the professor said, "that is precisely the difficulty."
"You must be exhausted." "Indeed. It's been a very long week."
"So you two have met." "Indeed we have."
"That's a bold claim." "Indeed it is — and I intend to defend it."

entries.meaning: Yes to something the speaker treats as following automatically from everything else. It is close to of course but drier, and in American use it very often carries a resigned "and of course that's what happened" about some predictable annoyance.
examples: "Did they charge you for the second bag?" "Naturally."
"Naturally, the one morning I forget an umbrella, it pours."
"Will you be at the wedding?" "Naturally. She's my sister."
"And the hardware store was closed when you finally got there." "Naturally."
"Naturally we'll cover the shipping," the manager said. "That was our mistake."

entries.meaning: Agreement that treats the point as beyond argument. As a standalone reply it is casual and confident; the longer without a doubt is the version that fits formal speech and writing.
examples: "That was the best game of the season." "No doubt."
"No doubt about it — he's the fastest kid on the team."
"You think traffic's gonna be bad?" "No doubt. It's a Friday before a holiday."
"Without a doubt the most talented person in the department."
"She earned that promotion." "No doubt. Nobody's arguing."

entries.meaning: Yes to something the speaker treats as obvious or automatic. 1. A warm, willing yes to a request. 2. Confirmation of something the listener should already have known — which, with the wrong tone, sounds condescending.
examples: "Could you hold the door?" "Of course."
"Do you remember me?" "Of course I do! You cut my hair for six years."
"Is the museum closed on Mondays?" "Of course — like every museum in the country."
"'Course I'll help you move. What time?"
"You didn't have to bring anything." "Of course I did. My mother raised me right."

entries.meaning: Enthusiastic agreement borrowed from Black church call-and-response: "keep saying what you're saying, because it's true." It endorses an opinion, usually a bold or frustrated one, and it belongs strictly to casual speech.
examples: "People need to learn how to merge." "Preach."
"Preach! Somebody finally said it."
"If they want us in the office, they can pay for parking." "Preach, sister."
She read the post out loud and her roommate just said, "Preach."
"Nobody needs eleven streaming subscriptions." "Preach it."

entries.meaning: The formal twin of exactly: it confirms that the other person has captured your meaning without error. It shows up in analytical and professional talk and can sound clipped or superior in casual company.
examples: "So the risk isn't the storm itself, it's the power loss." "Precisely."
"Precisely the point I was trying to make."
"You're suggesting the sample was contaminated?" "Precisely."
"Precisely so," the attorney said. "Nothing more, nothing less."
"Precisely what I have been telling this committee for two years," she said, and sat back down.

entries.meaning: Approving agreement with a distinctly 1960s-and-70s counterculture flavor that has never fully gone away. It says "I'm with you and I like what you just said," and older speakers use it straight while younger ones often use it with a wink.
examples: "I quit the job and I've never been happier." "Right on."
"Right on, man. Good for you."
"We're walking there instead of driving." "Right on. It's a nice night."
"She's going back to school at fifty-two." "Right on."
"Right on!" my uncle said, giving the guitarist a thumbs-up.

variants: say no more (the older, milder idiom)
entries.meaning: Recent slang, from African American English, meaning "I'm already convinced — you can stop explaining." It agrees and closes the topic in one move. It is at least as common in speech as in texting among speakers under about thirty, and it is out of place in any professional exchange.
examples: "There's free pizza in the conference room." "Say less."
"I can get us in without paying cover." "Say less, I'm on my way."
"It's a two-hour drive, but the beach is empty in October." "Say less."
"Say less — I'll bring the speaker."
"You don't have to explain the whole plot, I'll watch it." "Say less."

entries.meaning: Whole-hearted agreement with a friendly, unbuttoned feel. It confirms both facts and feelings, and it is one of the most common ways American speakers signal "same page as you" in relaxed conversation.
examples: "That commute would kill me." "Totally."
"Totally — I felt the exact same way when I first moved here."
"Do you think I overreacted?" "Totally not. Anyone would have said something."
"It's worth the extra money, don't you think?" "Oh, totally."
"Totally get it. No apology necessary."

entries.meaning: A one-word concession that the other person is right, often about something the speaker hadn't considered. Doubled — true, true — it becomes a mild, thinking-it-over agreement rather than a strong endorsement.
examples: "You'd have to leave at five to beat the traffic." "True."
"True, but that only works if the store's still open."
"It's cheaper to just cook at home." "True, true."
"Nobody actually reads the terms and conditions." "So true."
"True. I hadn't thought about the deposit."

entries.meaning: Agreement and acknowledgment from African American English, widely adopted in casual speech: "that's the truth" or, with rising pitch, "really?" Its heyday was the late 1980s and 1990s but it is still very much in use.
examples: "That show got way better in season two." "Word."
"I'm taking Friday off." "Word? Nice."
"Word up — that's exactly what I've been saying."
"Traffic on the bridge was insane this morning." "Word. Took me an hour."
He nodded once and said, "Word," and they bumped fists.

variants: don't have to tell me twice
entries.meaning: Wholehearted agreement with a statement, almost always a complaint. Like tell me about it, it means the opposite of what the words say — nobody actually wants it repeated. You said it is the shorter and more common spoken form; the full phrase sounds a touch more emphatic.
examples: "That was the worst flight of my life." "You can say that again."
"This week has felt about a month long." "You said it."
"You can say that again — I've been saying it for a year and nobody listened."
"Parking downtown is a nightmare." "You said it, brother."
"Somebody should have caught that before it went out the door." "You can say that again."

entries.meaning: A confident, faintly cocky yes: "obviously — you didn't even need to ask." It answers questions about the speaker's own plans, tastes, or abilities, and with a light tone it reads as friendly rather than boastful.
examples: "You going to the tailgate Saturday?" "You know it."
"Bet you're glad that's finally over." "You know it."
"Are you still doing the five a.m. workout thing?" "You know it. Every day."
"You already know," he said when I asked whether he'd saved me a seat.
"You're rooting for the underdog, aren't you?" "You know it."

entries.meaning: A compact, businesslike way to sign on to a statement or a proposal. It is at home in meetings, email threads, and negotiations, where it functions almost like a vote.
examples: "We should push the launch to April." "Agreed."
"Agreed — let's take the whole thing back to the drawing board."
"This can't happen again." "Agreed. I've already changed the process."
"Agreed on all three points. I'll write it up."
"Two weeks is too tight." "Agreed, but the client won't move."

entries.meaning: Agreement that concedes the point on its merits, usually after the speaker has briefly considered resisting. It is a graceful way to lose a small disagreement without making a production of it, and it fits a conference room and a kitchen table equally well.
examples: "It's cheaper, it's faster, and we already own the license." "Can't argue with that."
"No argument here. Let's go with the second option."
"If we leave now we beat the whole rush." "Hard to argue with that."
"Free is free." "Can't argue."
"You look like a man who needs a day off." "Can't argue with that," he said, laughing.

entries.meaning: Low-key approval of a plan or acceptance of a piece of news — one of the most-used acknowledgment words in casual American English. It signals "no objection" rather than enthusiasm, and learners should know that a bare cool in a text reads flat or faintly annoyed, the same way a bare k does.
examples: "I'll just meet you there at seven." "Cool."
"Dress code is whatever you want." "Cool, I'll wear jeans then."
"Cool — I'll let everybody know."
"Turns out we don't need the permit after all." "Oh, cool."
"Cool cool cool," he said, which meant he was quietly panicking.

entries.meaning: Acceptance of a bargain or a trade, spoken at the moment the terms are settled. It implies a two-sided arrangement, so it answers an offer rather than a statement of fact.
examples: "I'll cook if you do the dishes." "Deal."
"You get the front seat there, I get it back." "Deal."
"Fifty bucks and you throw in the case." "Deal."
"Deal," she said, and they shook on it.
"One episode, then bed." "Deal, but a long one."

entries.meaning: From the bookkeeping mark meaning "the same again." As an interjection it means "what he said goes for me too," so it works only when the previous statement could be repeated word for word by the speaker.
examples: "I'm exhausted." "Ditto."
"I thought the ending was a letdown." "Ditto. Felt rushed."
"Nice to finally meet you." "Ditto!"
"Ditto on the coffee — make mine black."
"I've got nothing on my calendar tomorrow." "Ditto, weirdly."

entries.meaning: Instant acceptance: the speaker treats the matter as already settled by saying so. It is punchier than deal and often signals that no negotiation is needed at all.
examples: "Would you be willing to swap weekends?" "Done."
"All I need is your signature by Friday." "Done. I'll sign it now."
"Can you take my name off the list?" "Consider it done."
"Just promise you won't tell my mother." "Done."
"Done and done," he said, crossing both items off the whiteboard.

entries.meaning: Concession rather than enthusiasm: "I may not fully agree, but your reason is good enough and I'll drop it." It is one of the most useful phrases in an American disagreement because it ends the argument without a loser. The clipped fair is the younger, slangier version.
examples: "I'd rather not drive at night." "Fair enough, I'll take the wheel."
"Fair enough — I hadn't considered the tax side of it."
"I just don't like horror movies." "Fair."
"We can't afford both this quarter." "Fair enough. Let's do the servers first."
"That's fair," he admitted. "I should have called."

entries.meaning: Acceptance with the enthusiasm drained out. 1. Neutral approval of an arrangement (Tuesday is fine). 2. Standing alone with falling intonation, it is famously reluctant — a surrender rather than an agreement, and Americans hear the difference instantly.
examples: "Does Tuesday work for you?" "Fine by me."
"Fine, we'll do it your way." (giving in)
"I'll be about twenty minutes late." "Fine, no rush."
"Fiiine, you can have the last slice."
"Is this seat okay?" "Fine, thanks."

entries.meaning: A concession token: the speaker accepts one piece of the other side's case, usually on the way to pressing their own. Standing alone it is a clean admission. Leading a sentence — Granted, it's expensive — it is almost always setting up a but, and American listeners hear that but coming.
examples: "It did come in under budget." "Granted."
"Granted, the first season is slow. Stay with it anyway."
"You've never actually driven one." "Granted — but I've read every review there is."
"I'll grant you that the timing was terrible."
"It's a lot of money." "Granted. It's also the last time we'll ever have to buy one."

entries.meaning: Agreement in form only. The speaker is dropping the argument without being convinced, and everyone in the room can hear it. This is one of the most reliably passive-aggressive phrases in American English — it is not a polite way to yield, and it should be used only when the sting is the point.
examples: "It's not that far — twenty minutes, tops." "If you say so."
"If you say so," she said, in a tone that said she did not say so.
"He swears he's cutting back." "If you say so."
"This is the good kind of surprise, I promise." "If you say so."
"The new system is so much simpler." "Sure, if you say so."

entries.meaning: Hedged, half-hearted agreement: "all right, but I'm not enthusiastic and I could be wrong." Americans use it constantly to soften a yes. Learners should know how weak it sounds — I guess in answer to an invitation reads as reluctance, not modesty, and hosts hear it that way.
examples: "Should we just walk from here?" "I guess. It's not that far."
"I guess so," he said. "I don't have a better idea."
"You're okay with the middle seat?" "I guess."
"So it's my turn to host this year." "I guess it is."
"That's the whole story?" "I guess, unless she left something out."

entries.meaning: Sympathetic acknowledgment: "your complaint registers with me and I'm not arguing." Note the hedge built into it — I hear you often precedes a but, and by itself it can mean "I understand your position" without conceding it.
examples: "This heat is unbearable." "I hear you. My AC's been running nonstop."
"I hear ya, man. Mondays are rough."
"I just want one weekend to myself." "I hear you, believe me."
"I hear you, but the deadline isn't moving."
"Nobody tells me anything around here." "I hear that."

entries.meaning: Excited agreement with an opinion the speaker already held — "yes, and I'm glad someone else said it." The tag right has question intonation but is not a real question; nobody expects an answer.
examples: "That trailer looked so bad." "I know, right?"
"I know, right? I thought I was the only one who noticed."
"Their prices have doubled." "I know, right? For the same sandwich."
She texted back "ikr" within about four seconds.
"It's way too cold in here." "Right? I've been saying that all week."

entries.meaning: Willing agreement to a plan — "count me in." The down surprises learners, because down elsewhere means sad or unavailable; here it is entirely positive, and I'm down to go and I'm down for that both mean an enthusiastic yes. It answers proposals, never statements of fact.
examples: "We're thinking tacos and then whatever's playing." "I'm down."
"Anybody want to drive up Saturday?" "I'm down, I've got nothing going on."
"Fair warning, it's a six a.m. start." "Still down."
"I'm game," she said, "as long as somebody else does the booking."
"Three days, no cell service, sleeping on the ground." "I'm in."

entries.meaning: An admission that the other person's objection landed and moved the speaker at least a little. It is the professional register's touché — standard in meetings, performance reviews, and arguments between adults who intend to keep working together afterward.
examples: "You've made that same complaint in three different meetings now." "Point taken."
"Point taken — I'll stop rewriting your emails before they go out."
"Maybe don't send those at midnight." "Point taken."
"Point taken," the director said. "We'll build in the extra week."
"It's hard to be a team player from behind a closed door." "Point taken. Door's open."

entries.meaning: From African American English. As a response it endorses what was just said as unvarnished truth; used at the front of a turn it announces that the speaker is about to drop the politeness and say what they actually think.
examples: "Half of these meetings could be an email." "Real talk."
"Real talk — I can't afford to live here much longer."
"Real talk, though: are you happy at that job?"
"He was never going to pay you back." "Real talk."
"Real talk, that was the best meal I've had all year."

entries.meaning: A workhorse. 1. Confirmation that a statement is correct. 2. A backchannel dropped repeatedly into someone else's explanation to show you are following. 3. At the head of a turn, a transition marker: "understood — now the next thing."
examples: "You're the one who called yesterday?" "Right, that was me."
"So you take the second exit—" "Right." "—and then go past the light."
"Right, let's get everyone back in the room."
"Right, right, I remember now."
"It's due on the fifteenth, right?" (here the tag is a question)

entries.meaning: Agreement by identification: "that describes me too." It began as internet shorthand but is now ordinary speech among younger Americans, so calling it internet slang undersells it — what it is not is professional. Same here is the older, register-neutral version that works in any conversation.
examples: "I'm not leaving the house today." "Same."
"I've had that song stuck in my head for three days." "Same, honestly."
"I don't understand a single thing about crypto." "Same here."
"Big same," she commented under the photo of the empty fridge.
"I'm gonna need a nap after this." "Same."

entries.meaning: The standard American way to approve a plan without fuss. It is the closing move of countless emails and text threads, pleasant enough for a client and casual enough for a friend.
examples: "Let's say two o'clock at the coffee place." "Sounds good."
"I'll send the draft tonight and you review it tomorrow." "Sounds good to me."
"We could just order in." "Sounds good — I'm too tired to cook."
"Sounds great. See you then."
"I'll pick you up at the north entrance." "Sounds good, I'll be outside."

entries.meaning: Emphatic agreement with a complaint, meaning the exact opposite of its literal words: "no need to explain — I've lived it." Learners sometimes take it as a real request for information, which produces a confusing conversation.
examples: "This traffic is ridiculous." "Tell me about it. I've been sitting here forty minutes."
"Airline food has gotten so bad." "You're telling me."
"Teenagers are expensive." "Tell me about it. Mine just needed braces."
"That software update broke everything." "Tell me about it."
"Moving is the worst." "Don't I know it. Third time in two years."

entries.meaning: Approving confirmation that somebody has finally arrived at the right idea or the right attitude — "yes, now you've got it." Warm and encouraging when the tone is right, condescending when it is not. Watch the context: there you go is also what Americans say while handing something over, which is a completely different move.
examples: "Okay, fine — I'll just ask them for the discount." "There you go."
"There you go — that's the first sensible thing anyone has said today."
"I'm taking the whole week off, actually." "There ya go. You've earned it."
"So it was the loose wire the entire time." "There you go."
"There you go," the coach said as the kid finally cleared the bar.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from fencing, where it acknowledges a hit. It concedes that the other person's comeback or counterargument landed — a good-humored admission of defeat on one specific point, not on the whole argument.
examples: "You're telling me to relax? You haven't sat down all day." "Touché."
"Touché. I walked right into that one."
"Says the guy who forgot his own anniversary." "Touché."
"You've never once cleaned the coffee maker." "Touché, I'll do it now."
"Touché," she laughed. "Point taken."

entries.meaning: The official radio and military yes, chosen because it cannot be confused with negative over a noisy channel. Civilians use it either in genuinely procedural contexts — pilots, dispatchers, police — or jokingly, to sound like a robot or a soldier.
examples: "Tower, confirm runway two-seven left." "Affirmative."
"Are you in position?" "Affirmative, we're a block out."
"Affirmative," the dispatcher replied. "Units are en route."
"Did you eat the last cookie?" "Affirmative," my brother said, deadpan.
"So we're agreed — nobody tells Mom until after the wedding." "Affirmative."

entries.meaning: A voting yes. In the United States it is the word used in legislatures, on boards, and at any meeting run on parliamentary procedure; outside of voting it survives mainly in nautical talk and in pirate imitations.
examples: "All in favor?" "Aye."
"The motion carries — twelve ayes, three nays."
"Aye," said the senator from Ohio.
"All those in favor of ordering pizza instead of cooking?" "Aye!" said all four kids at once.
"Aye, Captain," he said, mostly to make the kids laugh.

entries.meaning: The Navy's acknowledgment of an order, and it means something very specific: "I heard the order, I understand it, and I am carrying it out." Landlubbers use it playfully to accept an instruction, usually with a mock salute.
examples: "Raise the anchor." "Aye aye, sir."
"Aye aye, Captain," the ensign answered.
"Take out the trash before you go." "Aye aye," he sighed.
"Everyone in life jackets, please." "Aye aye!"
"Aye-aye," she said, saluting with a spatula.

entries.meaning: Item-by-item acknowledgment, taken straight from ticking boxes on a list: each check confirms that one more thing is present or done. It belongs to running through a list out loud — a packing list, a pre-flight, a recipe — and it does not work as an answer to an open question.
examples: "Passport?" "Check." "Boarding pass?" "Check."
"Tent, sleeping bags, bug spray." "Check, check, and check."
"Check," he said, and drew a line through the last item on the whiteboard.
"Did you put a hold on the mail?" "Check. Did it Tuesday."
Charger, headphones, something to read — check. I was ready four hours early.

entries.meaning: Radio language for "I received your message and understood it" — note that it confirms reception, not agreement. It has spread far beyond radios into ordinary workplace speech, where it sounds efficient and slightly clipped.
examples: "We're moving the truck to the loading dock." "Copy that."
"Copy. I'll meet you at the north gate."
"The client wants it in blue, not green." "Copy that, changing it now."
"Do not open that door until I say so." "Copy that."
"Copy," she said into the radio, "we're two minutes out."

entries.meaning: Confirmation that an explanation has landed. Gotcha is the relaxed spoken contraction, and be careful with it: in a different context gotcha! means "I caught you" or "I tricked you," so tone and situation decide which one a listener hears.
examples: "Turn left at the light, then it's the third house." "Got it."
"Gotcha — so the deposit isn't refundable."
"You have to log out and back in for it to take effect." "Got it, thanks."
"Don't mention the surprise party." "Gotcha."
"Got it," he said, scribbling the address on his hand.

entries.meaning: An acknowledgment that the information has been received and filed away. It is common in professional email and can be perfectly neutral — but standing alone in a reply it often reads as cool or faintly resistant, especially after criticism.
examples: "Please copy me on anything that goes to the client." "Noted."
"Duly noted. I'll make sure it's in the report."
"The deadline moved up a week." "Noted — thanks for the heads-up."
"You've been leaving the lights on again." "Noted."
"Noted," she wrote back, and nothing else, which told me plenty.

entries.meaning: From the old radio alphabet, where Roger stood for the letter R, for "received." Like copy, it confirms that a message came through. Outside radio work Americans use it as a brisk, mildly jokey "understood."
examples: "Head for the south entrance." "Roger that."
"Roger," the pilot answered. "Descending to eight thousand."
"Can you grab milk on your way home?" "Roger that."
"We need the room cleared by five." "Roger."
"Roger that, boss. Consider it handled."

entries.meaning: A CB and police radio code meaning "message received." Its 1970s trucker heyday left it in ordinary American speech as a playful, folksy way to say "got it," and today most people who say it are being at least a little tongue-in-cheek.
examples: "I'll have the report on your desk by noon." "Ten-four."
"Ten-four, good buddy — I'm right behind you."
"Pick the kids up at four, not four-thirty." "Ten-four."
"10-4," he typed, "on my way."
"Dispatch, we're clear on scene." "Ten-four, unit twelve."

entries.meaning: A formal acknowledgment of instructions, common in the military, in medicine, and in serious workplace conversations. It confirms comprehension and compliance at the same time, and its weight makes it sound grave in casual company.
examples: "This information does not leave this room." "Understood."
"Understood, sir. It won't happen again."
"You'll need to fast for twelve hours before the test." "Understood."
"Understood," the attorney said. "We'll file by Thursday."
"No overtime without written approval." "Understood."

entries.meaning: Formal assent to a request or an instruction, and in American English a distinctly stiff one. It lives in courtrooms, period dramas, and the mouths of fictional butlers; anywhere else an American says it, they are usually being mock-formal. Note the undertone: very well far more often signals reluctant compliance than actual agreement.
examples: "The court will hear from the defense first." "Very well, Your Honor."
"Very well. We'll proceed without him and send him the notes."
"I'd like to speak to your supervisor." "Very well, one moment."
"Very well then," he said, in a tone that made clear it was not.
"Then we'll pick this up on Monday." "Very well."

entries.meaning: Agreement to carry out a request — "consider it on my list." It answers instructions rather than statements, and it is one of the safest short replies in American workplace email.
examples: "Can you send me the numbers before the call?" "Will do."
"Will do — I'll have it to you within the hour."
"Whatever you do, don't let him talk you into the extended warranty." "Will do."
"Try to get some rest tonight." "Will do, doc."
"Will do!" she called over her shoulder.

entries.meaning: Cheerful compliance with a request, the house style of American servers, bartenders, and helpful coworkers. It also works as a warm reply to thank you and as confirmation that someone guessed right.
examples: "Could we get another round when you have a second?" "You got it."
"Thanks for squeezing me in today." "You got it."
"Two eggs, over easy, wheat toast." "You got it."
"So the meeting's at nine, not ten?" "You got it."
"You got it, boss," he said, already reaching for the box.

entries.meaning: A receipt token for a piece of information that clicks into place. Held longer (ahhh) it signals a fuller realization; clipped, it is a polite "I follow." Unlike oh, it suggests the news fits something the speaker already suspected.
examples: "Ah, so that's why the door wouldn't lock."
"She's his sister, not his wife." "Ah. That explains dinner."
"Ahhh, now I get it. The two forms look almost identical."
"It's pronounced EE-lee, not EYE-lee." "Ah, sorry."
"Ah, yes — I remember reading about that."

entries.meaning: An open-mouthed grunt on two beats, the second stressed and sharply higher; the vowels are not fixed, and some speakers say it closer to /əˈhɑ/. The discovery token — the sound of a problem coming apart in the speaker's hands. It is not a backchannel and not agreement, and swapping it for uh-huh is one of the more noticeable learner errors: uh-huh means "go on," while aha announces that the speaker has just understood something, usually with a change of posture to match.
examples: "Aha — the second copy was sitting in my drafts the whole time."
"Aha!" she said, fishing the missing screw out of the carpet.
"It only breaks when the file name has a space in it." "Aha."
"Aha, so that's why the two totals never matched."
He stared at the wiring diagram for a full minute before a quiet "aha" escaped him.

entries.meaning: A prompt for the rest of the story, with sharply rising intonation. 1. Impatient curiosity — "don't stop there." 2. Said flatly, it is dismissive: "so what?" The two are told apart entirely by tone, and the second one starts fights.
examples: "So I finally called her back." "And?"
"And? What did the doctor say?"
"I told him exactly what I thought of the whole plan." "And?" "And he quit."
"You're going to be late." "And?" (dismissive)
"They offered me the job." "And?!" "And I took it!"

entries.meaning: An explicit invitation to keep talking, used when a speaker has paused to check whether they still have permission. It is common from therapists, interviewers, and parents, and drawn out (ohhh, go on) it becomes flirtatious or falsely modest.
examples: "I don't want to bore you with the details." "Go on, I'm interested."
"Go on — what happened after she opened the letter?"
"So there were two problems with the design." "Go on."
"You're the best cook in this family." "Oh, go on." (mock modesty)
The detective nodded once. "Go on. Take your time."

variants: hmph (a different sound — a short annoyed snort through the nose)
entries.meaning: Not a spelled word but a hum through closed lips with a breathy onset; there is no vowel, and the pitch typically dips and comes back up. The thinking hum: where mm says "I'm listening," hm says "I'm weighing this," and it buys the speaker a beat before answering. Long and level it is genuine consideration; short and falling it is skepticism. Americans reliably read a lone hmm in a text message as bad news coming.
examples: "Hm. Let me think about that one."
"What if we moved the whole thing to Thursday?" "Hmm. That could actually work."
"Hmm," the mechanic said, which is never what you want to hear.
"He told me he'd already sent it." "Hm. That's not what my inbox says."
She wrote back a single "hmm" and I knew the answer was no.

entries.meaning: 1. With falling intonation, a small backchannel of interest: "that's news to me, and mildly interesting." 2. With rising intonation it is not agreement at all but a request for repetition ("what?"), and a bare huh? to a stranger or a boss can sound rude — sorry? or excuse me? is safer.
examples: "Turns out the building used to be a hat factory." "Huh. I had no idea."
"Huh, that's actually a pretty clever solution."
"They're closing the store in June." "Huh. Well, that stinks."
"Huh," he said, turning the box over in his hands.
"Your flight got moved to Terminal C." "Huh? Since when?"

entries.meaning: Acknowledgment that an explanation has been understood. It is a listening token with a slight formality to it — helpful on the phone and in professional talk — but delivered slowly and flatly it can imply disapproval or disbelief.
examples: "The charge is for the second bag." "I see. That wasn't on the confirmation."
"I see — so nothing ships until the payment clears."
"He's been out sick all week." "Ah, I see."
"I see," the interviewer said, writing something down.
"We changed the process in January." "I see. That would explain the confusion."

entries.meaning: A backchannel that pretends to be a question. It invites the speaker to keep going and shows mild surprise; said flatly, especially with a Southern drawl, it can carry a cool skepticism close to "we'll see about that."
examples: "He says he's going to run the whole marathon in under four hours." "Is that right?"
"Is that right? I never knew she grew up in Alaska."
"They're paying him twice what you make." "Is that right." (flat, unimpressed)
"The recipe's been in the family since 1890." "Is that so!"
"Is that right?" my grandfather said, which meant he did not believe a word of it.

entries.meaning: Not a spelled word but a closed-mouth hum on a single note; there is no vowel, so any respelling is an approximation. The most minimal listening noise in English, meaning little more than "I'm still here." A short flat mm is neutral attention; a long mmm over food is pleasure, and a falling mm with a lowered chin is doubt rather than agreement. Do not confuse it with mm-mm — two hums, the second one lower — which is the closed-mouth no.
examples: "So I told him we'd think about it—" "Mm." "—and he seemed fine with that."
"Mm," she said, eyes still on her book.
"Are you listening to me?" "Mm. Keep going."
"Mmm, this soup is incredible."
"You really think that's a good idea?" "Mmm…" (doubtful, trailing off)

entries.meaning: The closed-mouth yes: two hums through closed lips, the second one higher and stressed, with no vowel to spell. It affirms and backchannels at once, and Americans use it constantly on the phone. Two warnings for learners: with a flat, descending contour it turns cold and can mean "I heard you and I disagree," and as an answer to thank you it is the standard Southern-flavored "you're welcome."
examples: "You're coming Saturday, right?" "Mm-hmm."
"So I get off at exit 40—" "Mm-hmm." "—and you're the second driveway."
"Thanks so much for the ride." "Mm-hmm."
"Mhm," she texted back, which was somehow worse than nothing.
"Did you take your medicine?" "Mm-hmm," he said with his mouth full.

entries.meaning: 1. With rising intonation, genuine surprise: "seriously?" 2. With falling intonation, dry agreement with something obvious: "you don't say." The second one is gently sarcastic and very common in American conversation.
examples: "She's been promoted twice this year." "No kidding? Good for her."
"It's freezing in this office." "No kidding. I'm wearing two sweaters."
"No kidding — I ran into my third-grade teacher at the airport."
"Turns out the cheap tires wear out faster." "No kidding." (dry)
"They gave us an extra day to finish." "No kidding? That's a first."

entries.meaning: The basic receipt token of English: it marks the moment a speaker's state of knowledge changes. In this category it is the listener's way of saying "that's new to me," and a conversation in which one party never says oh sounds oddly flat to American ears.
examples: "The meeting got moved to Thursday." "Oh. Okay, thanks."
"Oh, I didn't realize you two knew each other."
"She's not coming — she's got the flu." "Oh, that's too bad."
"Ohhh, you meant the other Main Street."
"Oh," he said quietly, and you could hear him rearranging his whole afternoon.

entries.meaning: 1. Sudden remembering: "that's right, I'd forgotten." 2. Agreement with extra enthusiasm. 3. With rising intonation, oh yeah? is a challenge — "is that so?" — and in an argument it is a step toward a fight.
examples: "You said you'd call the plumber." "Oh yeah, I completely forgot."
"That place has amazing tacos." "Oh yeah, the best in town."
"Oh yeah? And who's going to stop me?" (challenge)
"Oh yeah, I remember him — tall guy, played bass."
"Do you like hiking?" "Oh yeah, we go almost every weekend."

entries.meaning: The workhorse backchannel of surprise and interest. 1. Rising, it asks the speaker to confirm and keep going. 2. Falling and flat, it is skeptical or unimpressed, and oh, really with a drawl is nearly always sarcastic.
examples: "They eloped in Vegas last weekend." "Really? Nobody told me."
"Really. And how much did that cost you?" (skeptical)
"I've never seen the ocean." "Really? Not once?"
"He says he never checks his phone at dinner." "Oh, really."
"It only took twenty minutes." "Really! I budgeted an hour."

entries.meaning: 1. Rising, it asks the speaker to confirm surprising news — really? with more disbelief in it. 2. Falling and flat, it is emphatic agreement with a complaint: "yes, and it's ridiculous." 3. Stressed hard and aimed at somebody, seriously? stops being a backchannel and becomes an accusation.
examples: "They cancelled the whole program." "Seriously? After two years of this?"
"Who parks across two spaces?" "Seriously."
"Seriously," he said, staring at the empty pot. "Every single morning."
"She got the promotion." "Seriously? Good for her."
"Srsly," my sister texted, "do not let him pick the restaurant again."

entries.meaning: The open-mouthed cousin of mm-hmm: an affirmative grunt, made with the jaw loose and the second syllable stressed and higher, that answers yes-or-no questions and keeps a conversation moving. It is not a synonym for aha, which announces a discovery rather than acknowledging one. A rapid, flat string of uh-huhs often signals impatience rather than attention.
examples: "Did you remember to lock up?" "Uh-huh."
"So you take 95 north—" "Uh-huh." "—for about ten miles."
"Uh-huh, uh-huh, and then what?"
"Are you even listening?" "Uh-huh." "Then what did I just say?"
"You'll be there by seven?" "Uh-huh, maybe earlier."

entries.meaning: Usually filed under surprise, but as a backchannel it does a specific job: it tells the speaker their news deserves a reaction. It is the listener's way of scoring a story as impressive, shocking, or bad — and a flat, delayed wow is a well-known way of expressing disapproval.
examples: "They drove the whole thing in one day — nineteen hours." "Wow."
"Wow, that's a lot of money for a used car."
"And then he just walked out in the middle of the meeting." "Oh, wow."
"Wow." She set down the letter. "I don't even know what to say."
"I told her the truth and she thanked me for it." "Wow, that's rare."

entries.meaning: 1. An old-fashioned expression of surprise that invites more of the story. 2. In modern American use it is far more often deadpan sarcasm aimed at something painfully obvious, so learners should assume the ironic reading unless the speaker is clearly delighted.
examples: "It turns out the cat had been in the garage the whole time." "You don't say!"
"Apparently it rains a lot in Seattle." "You don't say." (sarcastic)
"You don't say! Your mother and I went to that same hotel."
"The line is longer at lunchtime." "You don't say."
"He's forty and still lives with his parents." "Ya don't say."
